26.text: The architecture is still the same transformer, but JAX changes the style of thinking completely: from objects with hidden state to pure functions and explicit parameter passing.

27.text: Keep the task fixed so the real contrast is PyTorch's imperative style versus JAX's functional one.

28.text: This split already foreshadows JAX's philosophy: even randomness becomes explicit data you pass around instead of ambient framework state.

31.text: JAX is the same model seen through a different lens: no modules with internal state, just functions that transform inputs, parameters, and RNG keys.

32.text: The surface syntax looks NumPy-like, which is deceptive in a good way: beneath it sits a much more explicit functional execution model.

35.text: Keep the data order fixed so the conceptual jump to functional programming does not get muddied by run-to-run noise.

42.text: Download the names dataset from the internet if it is not already present locally.

45.text: URL pointing to the raw names dataset hosted in Karpathy's repository.

47.text: Read the text file and split it into individual name strings, one per line.

48.text: Randomize the training order so the model does not memorize sequences of names.

51.text: The set of unique characters in the dataset forms our vocabulary. Each character gets a fixed integer ID for the model to work with.

52.text: The beginning-of-sequence token doubles as the end-of-sequence marker for name boundaries.

53.text: The vocabulary has 27 tokens: 26 lowercase letters plus the BOS/EOS marker.

60.text: Split attention into 4 parallel heads so each can focus on different character relationships.

61.text: A single transformer layer, keeping the model minimal for this small-scale experiment.

62.text: Names up to 16 characters long fit in the context window. Longer names get truncated, but most fit easily.

63.text: Each of the 4 heads gets 4 dimensions of the 16-dimensional embedding, letting heads specialize on different character relationships.

68.text: JAX has no global random state: you create a key and split it for every random operation. jax.random.key is the modern typed constructor, where the key carries its generator implementation in its dtype; PRNGKey is the older raw uint32 pair. Same numbers, but a lab about explicit randomness may as well use the API JAX actually wants.

71.text: Parameter initializer, same N(0, 0.08) distribution, but using JAX's RNG.

72.text: JAX random requires an explicit key for every call. This makes randomness reproducible and parallelizable.

76.text: Derive the key count from the model rather than hard-coding it. Add a layer and the iterator below would otherwise run dry halfway through initialization.

77.text: Pre-split one key per parameter tensor. JAX forces you to say where every random number comes from, which is exactly what makes an initialization reproducible across devices.

78.text: Iterator over keys, each parameter gets its own unique key.

80.text: Parameters are a plain Python dict, no nn.Module, no parameter registration. In JAX, parameters are just data you pass to functions.

81.text: Initialize the token embedding table that maps each character to a learned vector.

82.text: Position embeddings give the model a sense of order. Each slot in the sequence has its own learned vector encoding 'where' a token sits.

83.text: The output head weight matrix that maps from embedding space back to vocabulary logits for next-token prediction.

85.text: Per-layer weights, same structure as previous labs, just stored in a dict.

86.text: Weight matrix that projects the normalized input into query vectors for attention.

87.text: Weight matrix that produces key vectors for positions to be matched against queries.

88.text: Weight matrix that produces value vectors carrying content to be mixed by attention.

89.text: Project the concatenated multi-head output back into the embedding space.

90.text: First MLP weight matrix that expands the representation to 4x the embedding dimension.

91.text: Second MLP weight matrix that compresses back to the original embedding dimension.

93.text: jax.tree.leaves extracts all arrays from the nested dict. JAX treats dicts as "pytrees", a core abstraction for working with nested parameter structures.

100.text: RMSNorm as a bare function, no class, no state. JAX style: functions in, functions out.

101.text: Mean of squares, same math as every other lab.

102.text: Divide by the root mean square to normalize. This keeps all vectors at roughly unit scale, preventing activations from growing or shrinking as they flow through layers.

105.text: The forward pass is a PURE FUNCTION: same inputs always produce the same outputs, no side effects. This is what makes jax.grad and jax.jit work, they need mathematical functions, not stateful objects.

111.text: Sequence length from the input shape.

112.text: Token embedding lookup via array indexing, same operation as PyTorch's nn.Embedding.

113.text: Position embeddings tell the model where each token sits in the sequence. Without these, the model would treat 'ab' and 'ba' identically.

114.text: Combine token and position embeddings and normalize before entering the transformer.

116.text: Iterate through each transformer layer. With one layer this runs once, but the code generalizes to deeper stacks.

117.text: Save the current hidden state so we can add it back after attention as a residual connection.

118.text: Normalize before the attention sub-layer. Pre-norm keeps activations stable so the attention mechanism receives well-scaled inputs.

120.text: Matrix multiply for Q projection. Explicit @ with the parameter array, no hidden weight storage.

121.text: Project the normalized input into key vectors that other positions will query against.

122.text: Project the normalized input into value vectors carrying content to aggregate.

125.text: Multi-head reshape, same transpose pattern as PyTorch.

126.text: Reshape keys into separate attention heads, matching the same multi-head pattern as queries.

127.text: Reshape values into separate attention heads for parallel processing.

129.text: Scaled dot-product attention. Same math, different framework.

130.text: Causal mask using JAX's array ops.

131.text: Apply mask with jnp.where, JAX's equivalent of PyTorch's masked_fill.

134.text: Multiply attention weights by value vectors. Tokens deemed relevant by the query-key scores contribute their content proportionally to the output.

135.text: Transpose and reshape heads back to (n, D).

136.text: Output projection + residual in one line.

139.text: Save the hidden state before the MLP for the second residual connection in this block.

140.text: Normalize before the feed-forward network, following the pre-norm transformer pattern.

141.text: Multiply by the expansion weights to widen the representation for richer transformations.

142.text: Apply ReLU activation to introduce nonlinearity between the two MLP linear layers.

143.text: Contract the MLP back to embedding dimension and add the residual. This completes the second sub-layer of the transformer block.

149.text: Loss function, also a pure function. Takes params, inputs, and targets; returns a scalar loss. This is exactly what jax.grad expects.

151.text: Run the forward pass inside the loss function. grad will differentiate through this entire computation.

152.text: log_softmax is numerically more stable than separate softmax + log.

153.text: Get the number of tokens in the input sequence for indexing into log probabilities.

154.text: Gather target log-probs and negate their mean. Cross-entropy in one expression.

161.text: Same hyperparameters as all previous labs.

162.text: jax.tree.map applies zeros_like to every array in the params dict. Functional alternative to manually creating matching zero buffers.

163.text: Second moment state, same pytree structure.

181.text: State in, state out. The whole step is a pure function of the parameters, the optimizer moments and the batch, which is what lets jit swallow it whole instead of compiling fragments with interpreted Python in between.

182.text: This is the transformation at the heart of JAX: value_and_grad(loss_fn) is a new function derived from the old one, not a method call on a tape. Using it instead of grad matters because the backward pass already computes the loss on its way through — grad alone would mean a second forward pass just to have a number to print.

183.text: First moment update. What was a Python for k in params loop in lab 02 is now one jax.tree.map: same arithmetic per leaf, but expressed as a single traced operation that stops caring how many parameter tensors there are.

184.text: Second moment: the moving average of squared gradients, which is what gives Adam its per-parameter step size.

185.text: Bias correction for the first moment, which starts at zero and would otherwise drag the early steps toward nothing.

186.text: The same correction for the second moment. Both are scalars here, computed once and broadcast over every leaf below.

188.text: The parameter update itself. Nothing is mutated: the lambda returns fresh arrays and the old ones simply stop being referenced.

193.text: Hand back the complete new state, loss included. The caller rebinds params, m_state and v_state on the next line, which is what "functional optimizer" reduces to in practice.

199.text: Train for 1000 steps, one document per step. Each iteration: forward, loss, grad, Adam update.

200.text: The instrument for this lab's real lesson. jit specializes on input shapes, and one name per step means the sequence length keeps changing, so this set records how many distinct programs XLA has been asked to build.

201.text: Two buckets: steps that paid for a compilation and steps that got a cache hit. Keeping them apart is what turns "jit is slow the first time" into a measurement.

203.text: Iterate over training steps, processing one name per step to update model parameters.

204.text: Cycle through the dataset with modular indexing. After seeing all names, we loop back for another pass.

205.text: Convert the name into a sequence of integer token IDs with BOS markers at both ends.

206.text: Clip to the maximum context window. Most names fit easily, but this guard prevents overflow on unusually long entries.

208.text: Convert the Python token list to a JAX array so it can flow through the JIT-compiled forward pass.

209.text: Wrap the target tokens as a JAX array. These are the correct next characters the model should learn to predict.

211.text: Ask the question before adding to the set, so the step can be attributed to the right bucket. A first-time shape and a cached shape run the identical Python.

214.text: Time the step from here, not from the top of the loop: tokenizing a name in Python would otherwise be mixed into a number meant to be about XLA.

215.text: One call does the forward pass, the backward pass and the Adam update. Compare lab 03, where those are three separate lines and three separate dispatches.

216.text: The linearly decayed learning rate is passed in as an argument rather than closed over. A Python float baked into the trace would be a compile-time constant, and a new value every step would mean a new compilation every step.

220.text: JAX dispatch is asynchronous: the call above returns as soon as the work is queued. Without blocking here we would be timing the enqueue, and every step would look impossibly fast.

221.text: Elapsed milliseconds for the step. On a first-time shape this includes tracing and compiling train_step; on a repeat it is only the compiled program running.

223.text: Announce the compilations as they happen. They are not confined to the start of training: this run traced new shapes at step 1, again at step 156, again at step 481.

225.text: One line per trace, with the length that triggered it. The corpus allows 14 lengths and a 1000-step run reaches 12 of them, so the same function gets built a dozen times, scattered throughout training rather than bunched at the front.

227.text: Everything else is a cache hit, and cache hits are where the compiled program finally pays for itself.

229.text: Print the loss periodically so we can monitor whether the model is learning.

235.text: The count that makes the gotcha concrete: twelve traces of one function, because the input shape kept changing under it.

236.text: Steps that had to compile, averaged. Roughly three orders of magnitude slower than the rest, which is why an unnoticed shape change in a JAX pipeline shows up as a mysterious stall rather than a gentle slowdown.

237.text: Steps that reused a compiled program, averaged, and the reason people love jit. The fix for the gap between these two numbers is to make shapes static by padding to one fixed length, which is exactly what lab 06 does.

242.text: Temperature 0.5 makes generation more conservative: the model favors high-confidence predictions, producing more typical-sounding names.

244.text: Sampling needs randomness too, so inference gets its own key to thread through the loop. Nothing is ambient in JAX, not even at generation time.

245.text: Generate 20 brand-new names by sampling from the model's learned distribution.

246.text: Begin each generated name with the beginning-of-sequence token as the initial prompt.

247.text: Generate one character at a time, up to the maximum sequence length. Each step feeds all generated tokens back through the model.

248.text: Convert growing token list to JAX array.

249.text: Forward pass, the same pure function, just called without gradient tracking.

250.text: Grab the logits for the last generated position and divide by temperature. Lower values make the distribution sharper and more predictable.

251.text: jax.random.split produces two new keys from one, JAX's way of consuming randomness without hidden state. Every random call needs a unique key.

252.text: categorical samples from log-probabilities (unnormalized logits). JAX's equivalent of PyTorch's multinomial.

253.text: When the model outputs the BOS token during generation, it signals the name is complete and we stop adding characters.

255.text: Append the newly sampled token to the growing list so it becomes part of the context for predicting the next character.

256.text: Map each token ID back to its character, skipping the leading BOS, to assemble the generated name as a readable string.

257.text: Print the finished name. The model assembled it from the 1000 names it saw during training, one per step, out of the 32K in the corpus.
